title: The Swan Who Answered the Kumaras
subtitle: Brahma's oldest sons meet the hamsa
story:
Sanaka and his brothers were the oldest minds in creation, born directly from Brahma's thought — and they carried a question that no one, not even their father, could answer.

They came to Brahma's abode and asked him for the subtle goal of yoga: the end that all practice points toward and never quite reaches. Brahma, the creator of worlds, sat with their question for a long time. He did not answer from the wealth of his own knowledge. Instead he turned his attention inward and meditated on Krishna. And Krishna, seeing what was needed, appeared before the sages in the form of a swan.

A great white hamsa came gliding into that assembly, calm as the water it had crossed. The four sages rose, walked up to it, and bowed at its feet. Who are you, they asked, that we should be answered by a bird? The swan's reply did not begin with a teaching. It began by turning the question back on them. If in truth there is no difference in the self, it said, then your question has no ground. Know that I alone am, and nothing apart from me.

Then, because they had asked, it taught them.

Look at the mind, said the swan. It runs into the qualities of nature, and the qualities run into it; the more it serves them, the deeper it sinks. Waking, dreaming, and dreamless sleep are only states of the intellect, spun out of those qualities. Bondage is nothing else: the self forgets itself and sees many where there is one. So long as the sense of difference does not turn back, the knot holds. And yet the one who enjoys the objects of waking, who recollects them in dream, who withdraws from both in deep sleep — that one is the same throughout, the knower behind the senses, untouched by what passes before it.

Cut the knot in the heart with the sword of knowledge, said the swan. See the world for what it is — the play of the mind, like the circle of fire a burning brand traces when you whirl it. One light, and the eye believes a ring of flame. So the one reality appears as many, and the dream of waking, dreaming, and sleeping is woven from nothing but the mind's own activity.

Withdraw the gaze, then. Turn from thirst. Sit in silence and taste the bliss that is simply your own self. The body is a perishable thing, put on and taken off like a garment, and the man who has woken to his own nature watches the exchange without confusion, as a drunken man hardly notices a change of clothes. Even the body's comings and goings are governed by the acts that set it in motion; the one established in awareness does not return to the dream once the reality is seen.

This, said the swan, is the secret of sankhya and yoga, the two great paths of knowledge and practice. I am the essence of yoga, the essence of sankhya, the essence of truth, of the right, of radiance. All the qualities of nature serve me, who am beyond them, wanting nothing. And the sages Sanaka and his brothers felt their doubt fall away, as a knot loosens under patient fingers. They worshipped the swan and praised it, and the praise and the worship rose in the air of Brahma's hall like a tide.

Krishna, telling all this to Uddhava long afterward, let the story rest there. That was the form his disciples had asked about, the hamsa that comes and goes upon the water of the mind. The question the Kumaras had carried from the very beginning of creation dissolved not in an answer but in the seeing of who it was that asked — and the swan, having done its work, was gone, leaving only the stillness it had pointed to.
reflection: The swan's first reply is the whole teaching in miniature: before the question about the goal of yoga can be asked, the questioner must see who is asking. Krishna does not satisfy the Kumaras' curiosity so much as dissolve the position their question comes from, and the oldest sages in creation are the ones who finally learn it.
next_story_tease: From the swan, Krishna turned to a man of Avanti whose loss of everything had taught him the same lesson.
hero_scene: A great white swan glides into the hall of Brahma's abode; the four ancient sages bow at its feet while Brahma watches from his seat, and the swan's head is turned toward them as if about to speak.
